about.subtitle: A national vision to empower talent and support the state
about.text: Kayan Shabab Misr is a youth political institution founded in 2018, inspired by the National Youth Conferences and the political leadership's call to develop Egyptian political life. It brings together academic and professional youth to offer a different public-service experience that unites young people, raises constitutional awareness, and genuinely prepares them for decision making.

items.q: Who are we, and what is Kayan Misr?
items.a: Kayan Misr is a national youth party founded in 2018 that spreads constitutional culture and prepares young cadres for public and parliamentary work.
To build an aware generation able to take an active part in political life and support state institutions in line with Egypt Vision 2030.

items.q: What are the official membership requirements?
items.a: Applicants must be Egyptian citizens in full possession of their civil rights and committed to Kayan's principles and bylaws.

items.q: How do registration and selection work?
items.a: Apply through the online membership form; the membership committee then contacts you for an introductory interview.

items.q: What volunteer and research opportunities are available?
items.a: Members can join specialized committees, research teams, event organization, and simulation and training programs.

intro.title: Youth voices at the National Dialogue table
intro.text: Kayan Misr takes part in National Dialogue sessions with trained youth delegations that carry young people's views and proposals to every track, and follows up on implementing the recommendations with the relevant bodies.
points: Submitting youth proposals through well-researched working papers.
Holding preliminary listening sessions in the governorates before each round.
Tracking dialogue outcomes and measuring their real-world impact.

dialogue.axesSubtitle: We take part in all three tracks of the National Dialogue through specialized member committees.

axes.title: Political track
axes.text: Political rights, the electoral system, local government, human rights, and public freedoms.

axes.title: Economic track
axes.text: Inflation and prices, private investment, industry and agriculture, and public debt.

axes.title: Social track
axes.text: Education and health, culture and national identity, family and social cohesion, and youth.

sessions.title: The Local Administration Law and youth participation in councils
Entrepreneurship and small business financing for youth

initiatives.title: Everyone has something to offer
initiatives.subtitle: A system that brings together people, expertise, and services, turning individual abilities into mutual benefit.

items.title: Time Bank
items.idea: Every hour of service you give another member earns you an hour of credit, which you later spend on a service from a different member — no money changes hands.
list: An engineer spends an hour helping someone read an engineering drawing.
They earn one hour of credit.
They spend it on an hour of English lessons or tech support.
The platform records balances and keeps a log of every exchange.
items.value: Turning people's time and skills into a community resource, even for those who can't pay.
items.challenge: Ensuring service quality, preventing fake accounts, and balancing the services requested with those offered.

items.title: Legal Clinic
items.idea: A platform that helps citizens understand official papers, find the right procedure and the competent authority, and use their right to appeal or file complaints.
list: The citizen uploads the document or describes the problem.
They get a plain-language explanation of the terms and procedures.
They learn the competent authority, the required documents, and the legal deadlines.
They can request a review by a volunteer or specialist lawyer.
They get guidance on filing a complaint or appeal through official channels, such as the Unified Government Complaints System when it's the right body.
items.value: Narrowing the gap between citizens and their legal rights.
items.challenge: Protecting documents and personal data, reviewing information legally, and never giving misleading automated answers or guaranteeing case outcomes.

items.title: Skills Bank
items.idea: An organized database of experienced professionals ready to give their time and knowledge to serve the community or institutions.
list: An engineer gives an initial technical review of a community project.
An accountant helps an NGO organize its budget.
A marketing specialist helps a small business define its audience.
A doctor takes part in a health awareness activity.
items.note: The bank can run on hours, direct volunteering, or free consultations depending on each service.
items.value: Putting existing expertise to use instead of leaving much of it untapped.
items.challenge: Verifying qualifications, defining the scope of each consultation, and avoiding conflicts of interest.

items.title: The Party's Advisory Arm
items.idea: A network of experts and specialists offering free consultations to citizens, and helping study public problems and draft actionable proposals.

tracks.title: Serving citizens

items.value: Turning professional expertise into public service, and linking individual problems to institutional solutions.

ministryStructure.title: How a ministry is organized
ministryStructure.subtitle: Egyptian ministries share a similar structure; the sectors and affiliated bodies differ from one ministry to another.

levels.title: The minister
levels.text: Sets and oversees the ministry's policy, accountable to the prime minister and the House.

levels.title: Deputy ministers and the minister's office
levels.text: Deputies handle specific portfolios, supported by a technical office and advisers.

levels.title: Sectors
levels.text: Each led by a sector head or first undersecretary, covering a main area of the ministry's work.

levels.title: Central and general departments
levels.text: Executive units inside each sector, divided into general departments and departments.

levels.title: Governorate directorates
levels.text: The ministry's executive arms in each governorate, working with the governor.

levels.title: Affiliated bodies
levels.text: Public authorities, companies and research centres under the ministry, each with its own management.

parties.title: Parties in the House of Representatives
parties.subtitle: Seat distribution after the 2025 elections (results announced January 2026).

ngos.title: Civil society organizations
ngos.subtitle: Civil work in Egypt is governed by Law No. 149 of 2019 on Regulating Civil Work and its executive regulations, supervised by the Ministry of Social Solidarity.
ngos.typesTitle: Forms of civil work under the law

types.title: Associations
types.text: An organized group of natural or legal persons pursuing a non-profit purpose.

types.title: Foundations
types.text: Created by allocating funds to a non-profit purpose.

types.title: Sectoral and regional unions
types.text: Bring together associations working in one field or one region.

types.title: General Union of NGOs
types.text: The umbrella body for civil work nationwide.

types.title: Foreign NGOs
types.text: Licensed to operate in Egypt under the law's conditions.

steps: Draft the bylaws and define the field of work and geographic scope.
Submit the notification and documents to the administrative body at the Ministry of Social Solidarity.
The association gains legal personality upon notification unless the authority objects within the legal period.
Open a bank account in the association's name and keep the required records and periodic reports.
rules: No partisan political activity or funding of parties or candidates.
Funds may only serve the association's purposes.
Foreign funding requires notifying the administrative body and following the law.
examples: National Alliance for Civil Development Work

governors.title: Governors
governors.subtitle: Governors of the 27 governorates after the 16 February 2026 reshuffle.

governorateStructure.title: How a governorate is organized
governorateStructure.subtitle: Set by Local Administration Law No. 43 of 1979 and its amendments, the same in every governorate.

levels.title: The governor
levels.text: Represents the executive branch in the governorate, appointed by the president, and oversees public policy and utilities.

levels.title: Deputy governor
levels.text: Assists the governor and handles delegated files.

levels.title: Secretary-general and assistant
levels.text: Run the governorate's administrative apparatus and follow up on decisions.

levels.title: Executive council
levels.text: The governor, deputies, heads of districts and cities, and directorate heads, following development plans and services.

levels.title: Service directorates
levels.text: Ministry branches in the governorate: education, health, housing, agriculture, social solidarity and more.

levels.title: Local units
levels.text: Districts (markaz), cities, neighbourhoods and villages, each with a head and a unit running daily services.

governorateStructure.note: The constitution (Article 180) provides for elected local councils; none have been elected since they were dissolved in 2011.

simulations.title: Simulation models
simulations.subtitle: Participants step into the roles of real officials and run realistic sessions under the constitution and the governing laws.

models.title: Government simulation
models.subtitle: The Cabinet
models.about: Participants run a cabinet meeting on a public issue or crisis and come out with actionable decisions and policies.
stages: Presenting the issue or crisis to the cabinet
Each minister prepares a policy paper for their sector
Cabinet meeting and discussion
Deciding, assigning responsibilities and budget
Government statement and press conference

models.title: House of Representatives simulation
models.subtitle: The legislature
models.about: Participants act as MPs in lawmaking and oversight: from tabling a bill to voting on it, plus using oversight tools.
stages: Tabling a government bill or a member's bill
Discussion in the competent committee
Preparing the committee report
Plenary debate and vote
Oversight session: questions, briefing requests and interpellations

models.title: Senate simulation
models.subtitle: Formerly the Shura Council
models.about: Participants study matters referred to the Senate and give its opinion, such as laws complementing the constitution and the development plan.
stages: Referral of the matter to the Senate
Study in the competent committee with expert hearings
Preparing a report with opinion and proposals
Plenary discussion of the report
Sending the Senate's opinion to the President or the House

models.title: Governor simulation
models.subtitle: The governorate executive council
models.about: Participants run a virtual governorate: receiving citizens' complaints, chairing the executive council and handling a service crisis.
stages: Reviewing citizens' complaints or a service crisis (water, roads, building violations)
Executive council meeting and assigning responsibilities
Drafting an action plan with a timeline and budget
A virtual field follow-up visit
The governor's report on results
models.reference: Egyptian Constitution: Articles 175 – 183 (Local Administration) — Local Administration Law No. 43 of 1979

models.title: Local popular council simulation
models.subtitle: Popular oversight of local government
models.about: Participants form an elected local council that follows the development plan in its area and oversees executive bodies with real oversight tools.
roles: Members (a quarter youth, a quarter women, at least half workers and farmers)
stages: Discussing the local development plan and budget
Submitting proposals, questions and briefing requests
Interpellating the head of the local unit
Voting on recommendations or a no-confidence motion
Following up on implementation
